svg.text: Offline Hash Cracking — Attack Modes vs. the Hash's Work Factor
loop: guess a candidate → hash it → compare to the target → repeat, at N guesses/second
Attack modes — narrow & cheap → broad & costly
1 · Dictionary
a wordlist (rockyou) → catches reused / common passwords
2 · Dictionary + Rules (most fall HERE)
mutate each word: summer2024 → Summer2024! → S0mm3r24
3 · Mask / Hybrid
enumerate a PATTERN: ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d?d?d = Summer2024
4 · Brute-force
every combination — exponential; the last resort
The speed wall (same GPU)
guesses/sec depends on the HASH, not the password:
MD5 / NTLM (fast)
~58,000,000,000 /s → weak pw cracked in seconds
bcrypt cost 12 (slow)
~9,000 /s → 6 MILLION× slower
time = keyspace ÷ guesses/sec
slow hash × high-entropy password = not crackable.
The two crackers — same job, different engine
John the Ripper — CPU-first · hundreds of hash formats · a powerful RULES engine · "incremental" (Markov) mode.
Reach for John for format breadth (NetNTLM, Kerberos, ZIP, PDF) and clever rule-based guessing on a CPU.
Hashcat — GPU-first · raw throughput (billions/sec) · the mask/hybrid king · one `-m` mode per hash type.
Reach for Hashcat when you have a GPU and a fast hash: masks make brute-force TARGETED, not blind.
Feed them the right hash type with name-that-hash / hash-identifier → set John's --format or Hashcat's -m.
Truth #1: most real passwords fall to dictionary + RULES, not brute force — humans are predictable.
Truth #2: the defender's only real lever is the hash's work factor (bcrypt/argon2 + salt), not "complexity rules".
